z-m-22-01.title: What remains when x to the 2026th power is divided by x²−1?
z-m-22-01.topic: Division identities and the rule for remainders (powers)
z-m-22-01.goal: Using the values that make the divisor 0, confirm why a rule for remainders guessed from a few examples also holds for large powers, and apply it when dividing by another quadratic expression.
z-m-22-01.material: When x^n (the expression with x multiplied n times, n a natural number) is divided by the quadratic expression x²−1, it can be written as x^n=(x²−1)Q(x)+R(x), and the remainder R(x) is an expression of degree at most 1 (including constants). Looking at the results for n = 1, 2, 3, ... one by one, let's think about the remainder when n=2026. "x to the 2026th power" is the expression with x multiplied 2026 times.
z-m-22-01.thinking.0: Telling apart guessing a rule from being sure of it
z-m-22-01.thinking.1: Adjusting how sure you are in your judgment as information increases
z-m-22-01.thinking.2: Finding the reason and generalizing to other cases
z-m-22-01.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-01.prereq.1: Experience of writing polynomial division in the form A=BQ+R (the degree of R is lower than the degree of B)
z-m-22-01.prereq.2: The sign of powers of (−1) (1 when multiplied an even number of times, −1 when multiplied an odd number of times)
z-m-22-01.s.s1.prompt: Let's look at how the judgment about the remainder of x^n divided by x²−1 changes as information increases.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the remainders in the table side by side together with whether n is odd or even.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.hint.1: Each time new information comes out, write in one word whether your judgment "became more convinced, changed, or stayed the same".
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.info:
Result of dividing directly (only the remainder is written)
n=1: x¹ = (x²−1)·0 + x → remainder x
n=2: x² = (x²−1)·1 + 1 → remainder 1
n=3: x³ = (x²−1)·x + x → remainder x
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only the information you have now, what do you think the remainder is when n=2026?
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Both the guess "1 if even, x if odd" and the judgment that you want to see more examples are reasonable right now. But three examples are only a basis for a guess, not a proof.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 1 (it seems 1 remains when n is even)
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You are guessing the rule that x and 1 alternate, x for odd and 1 for even.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: x (the x from n=1 keeps remaining)
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not put the result from n=2 into the rule.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is too early to decide. I want to see more examples like n=4, 5
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You are aware that there are only three examples and are putting off the judgment.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: In the remainders of the three lines, you do not see the coefficient growing. You made a rule that differs from the observation.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.info:
Results of dividing further
n=4: x⁴ = (x²−1)(x²+1) + 1 → remainder 1
n=5: x⁵ = (x²−1)(x³+x) + x → remainder x
All five examples match "x if odd, 1 if even".
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How much can you trust the guess "if n=2026, the remainder is 1" right now?
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.after: As examples increase, the guess gets firmer, but whether it holds for every n has to be confirmed by a reason.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is proven now. It was right all five times, so it must hold
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even with more examples, "every n" has not been confirmed. You need to know why it holds for large n too.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: My belief has grown, but I do not know why, so it is not settled
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You are distinguishing the number of examples from having a reason.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: n=2026 is too big, so predicting is meaningless
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If you give up predicting just because n is big, you cannot use the rule. First think about whether you can find a reason.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Five is not enough, so I divide directly all the way to n=2026 to check
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Dividing directly is not realistic. Think about whether there is a way to find a reason.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Let's find the reason. The remainder has degree at most 1, so we can write R(x)=ax+b. In x^n=(x²−1)Q(x)+ax+b, x²−1=(x−1)(x+1), so (x²−1)Q(x) becomes 0 whether you plug in 1 or −1 for x. Then 1=a+b and (−1)ⁿ=−a+b remain.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Using this information, find the remainder when n=2027.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If n=2027, then (−1)ⁿ=−1, so a+b=1 and −a+b=−1, giving a=1, b=0, so the remainder is x. In the same way, for n=2026, a=0 and b=1, so the remainder is 1.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check whether you calculated (−1)ⁿ as 1, as for n=2026.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Check the sign of a in 1=a+b.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You used both equations to find a and b.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If it is x+1, compare what a+b is with 1=a+b.
z-m-22-01.s.s1.reflect: At first you guessed the rule from three examples, and as examples increased your belief grew, but your certainty came from the reason that "the divisor becomes 0 at x=1 and x=−1". You may keep your first guess, but look at how the basis for it changed from "the number of examples" to "a reason".
z-m-22-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's use the same method for the case of dividing x to the 2026th power by x²−4. (x²−4=(x−2)(x+2)) What is the remainder?
z-m-22-01.s.s2.hint.0: In the same order as for x²−1, write the values at 2 and at −2.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.hint.1: First decide whether (−2) to the 2026th power is positive or negative.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.o.a: 1 (only the divisor changed, so the result is the same)
z-m-22-01.s.s2.r.a: When the divisor changes, the values that determine the remainder (here, the values at 2 and −2) also change.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.r.b: The constant term of the divisor does not simply become the remainder.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.o.c: 2²⁰²⁶·x (a power of 2 is attached to the x term)
z-m-22-01.s.s2.r.c: Check what happens to the coefficient of the x term when the two values from x=2 and x=−2 are equal.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.o.d: 2²⁰²⁶ (only a constant remains and there is no x term)
z-m-22-01.s.s2.r.d: You found a and b also using the fact that the values at x=2 and x=−2 are equal.
z-m-22-01.s.s2.explain: Writing the remainder as ax+b and plugging in x=2, −2 gives 2²⁰²⁶=2a+b and (−2)²⁰²⁶=−2a+b, and since the two values are equal, a=0 and b=2²⁰²⁶.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, "The rule was right five times, so of course it is right for n=2026 too." Explain to your friend why you can be sure the rule also holds for large n.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write in this explanation what the values of x are that make the divisor 0.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write what (−1)ⁿ is when n is odd and when n is even, and continue.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If we write the remainder as ax+b, ...
z-m-22-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write knowing why the remainder is written in the form ax+b (degree at most 1)?
z-m-22-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you persuade with "there is a reason" rather than "it was right five times"?
z-m-22-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write why the cases of n even and n odd split?
z-m-22-01.s.s3.model.0: Let the remainder be ax+b, and plugging x=1 and x=−1 into x^n=(x²−1)Q+ax+b gives 1=a+b and (−1)ⁿ=−a+b. If n is even, (−1)ⁿ=1, so a=0 and b=1, and no matter how many times we checked, n=2026 also gives 1.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.model.1: Being right five times is only a guess. The divisor is (x−1)(x+1), so it becomes 0 at x=1 and x=−1, and with those two values we can fix the coefficients of the remainder. The sign of (−1)ⁿ splits depending on odd and even, so the reason for the rule is confirmed.
z-m-22-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that persuades with a reason instead of adding more examples

z-m-22-02.title: x⁴+4 has no real roots, but can it be written as a product?
z-m-22-02.topic: Factoring (the relationship between roots and factors, transforming by adding and subtracting a term)
z-m-22-02.goal: Verify the generalization "if there are no roots, it cannot be factored" with a counterexample and a specific transformation, and make expressions of your own for which the same method works.
z-m-22-02.material: We talk within the range where the coefficients of polynomials are real numbers. Jihu said, "There is no real x that satisfies x⁴+4=0. So x⁴+4 cannot be factored." Let's check whether we can believe Jihu's statement as it is. ("x⁴" is read as "x to the fourth power".)
z-m-22-02.thinking.0: Finding a counterexample to a generalization
z-m-22-02.thinking.1: Revising a judgment based on new information
z-m-22-02.thinking.2: Making examples of your own that satisfy the conditions
z-m-22-02.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-02.prereq.2: Experience factoring quadratic expressions of the form ax²+bx+c
z-m-22-02.s.s1.prompt: Let's look at how the judgment about the claim "if there are no real roots, it cannot be written as a product" changes as new information comes in.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write separately whether each piece of information touches the "general claim" or touches "x⁴+4 itself".
z-m-22-02.s.s1.hint.1: Expand the given expression yourself and check whether it equals the original expression.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.info: x⁴ is at least 0, so x⁴+4 is always at least 4. That is, there is no real x for which x⁴+4=0. If a linear expression x−k is a factor, the value of the expression must be 0 at x=k, so there is no linear factor with real coefficients.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only the current information, how do you judge whether x⁴+4 can be written as a product of two or more expressions with real coefficients?
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.after: It has been confirmed that there is no linear factor, but the possibility of a product of two quadratic expressions is still open. For now, it is reasonable to hold your judgment or to leave the possibility open.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It cannot be written. There is no linear factor, so it does not split into quadratic expressions either
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You jumped from the fact that there is no linear factor to "no product works". Did you consider whether a product of two quadratic expressions is possible?
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It cannot be decided yet. The possibility of a product of two quadratic expressions remains
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You are distinguishing having no linear factor from not splitting into a product.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It can be written. If 4 is added, it always splits
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It does not split just because 4 is added. You need a fact as a basis.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It can be written. Expressions with an even power all split
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: x²+1 is also an expression with an even power, but it does not split into linear expressions with real coefficients. Think of a counterexample.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.info: The similar expression x⁴+5x²+4 also has no real roots because x⁴+5x²+4≥4. But if you view x² as A, then A²+5A+4=(A+1)(A+4), so x⁴+5x²+4 can be written as (x²+1)(x²+4).
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you judge Jihu's general claim, "if there are no real roots, it cannot be written as a product"?
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.after: x⁴+5x²+4 has no real roots but still splits into (x²+1)(x²+4), so Jihu's general claim does not hold. But that does not prove that x⁴+4 splits.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The general claim is broken. But whether x⁴+4 splits must be checked separately
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You are distinguishing that one counterexample breaks a general claim, and whether a particular expression splits is a separate matter.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Now x⁴+4 can surely be written as a product too
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A counterexample only breaks the general claim; it does not guarantee that x⁴+4 splits.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Jihu's claim is still right. x⁴+5x²+4 is a different expression
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: "If there are no real roots, it does not split" is a statement about all expressions, so one other expression is a counterexample.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: x⁴+5x²+4 was split by changing x² to A, so it cannot be used as a counterexample
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Expand (x²+1)(x²+4) and check yourself whether it equals the original expression.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.info: If you add and subtract 4x² in x⁴+4, then x⁴+4=(x⁴+4x²+4)−4x²=(x²+2)²−(2x)².
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: How can you write x⁴+4 with this transformation?
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.after: (x²+2)²−(2x)²=(x²+2−2x)(x²+2+2x)=(x²−2x+2)(x²+2x+2). Check whether expanding gives x⁴+4. Even without real roots, it can be written as a product of two quadratic expressions.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: (x²+2)²−(2x)² has a different value from x⁴+4, so it cannot be used
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Expand (x²+2)² and subtract 4x², and calculate whether you get x⁴+4.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: (x²+2)²−(2x)²=(x²+2)−(2x), so it becomes one quadratic expression
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A difference of squares is (A−B)(A+B), and it does not become the single expression A−B.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It becomes the product of two quadratic expressions, (x²−2x+2)(x²+2x+2)
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You learned the method of changing a difference of two squares into a product.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is a difference of two squares, so it does not split further in the real numbers
z-m-22-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: A²−B²=(A−B)(A+B) holds whatever expressions A and B are.
z-m-22-02.s.s1.reflect: At first, the fact that there is no linear factor was not enough to reach a conclusion. As the counterexample and the specific transformation appeared, the judgment became settled. If you first guessed "it does not split", say what information changed that thought.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.prompt: Let's make expressions x⁴+c² for which the same method as for x⁴+4 works within integer coefficients. When rewriting x⁴+c² in the form (x²+c)²−(dx)², what relationship must c and d have? Find two different pairs where c and d are natural numbers and c is at least 3.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.hint.0: Expand (x²+c)² and compare which term differs from x⁴+c².
z-m-22-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what number the leftover term must be the square of, and after choosing d, calculate c.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.ok.c1: c is at least 3 and d is a natural number.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.fail.c1: c must be at least 3 and d must be at least 1.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.fail.c2: c and d must be integers.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.fail.c3: (x²+c)²=x⁴+2cx²+c², so (dx)² and 2cx² must be equal. Compare d² and 2c.
z-m-22-02.s.s2.explain: x⁴+c²=(x²+c)²−2cx², so if 2c is the square of an integer d², it splits into (x²−dx+c)(x²+dx+c). (c, d)=(8, 4) gives x⁴+64=(x²−4x+8)(x²+4x+8), (18, 6) gives x⁴+324=(x²−6x+18)(x²+6x+18), and (32, 8) gives x⁴+1024=(x²−8x+32)(x²+8x+32). If real coefficients are allowed, it splits for every positive c with d=√(2c), but if limited to integers, this kind of relationship is needed.

z-m-22-03.title: What more can we learn from the fact that the remainders are the same?
z-m-22-03.topic: Using the remainder theorem (remainders from several linear expressions)
z-m-22-03.goal: Work out how the judgment about the remainder on division by a quadratic expression changes as facts about remainders are added one at a time, and make several expressions of your own that satisfy the same conditions.
z-m-22-03.material: f(x) is a polynomial with real coefficients and its degree is not known. Polynomial division is written in the form f(x)=(divisor)·(quotient)+(remainder), and the degree of the remainder is lower than the degree of the divisor. As facts become known one at a time, let's look at what can be said about the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2).
z-m-22-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-22-03.thinking.1: Telling apart when new information changes the judgment and when it does not
z-m-22-03.thinking.2: Making several expressions that satisfy the conditions
z-m-22-03.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-03.prereq.1: Experience writing the remainder of a polynomial divided by a linear expression in the form f(x)=(divisor)(quotient)+remainder
z-m-22-03.s.s1.prompt: Let's look at how my judgment about the remainder on division by (x−1)(x−2) changes as facts about remainders are added one at a time. (The degree of f(x) is not known.)
z-m-22-03.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite each fact as an equation about a value, like "f(1)=…".
z-m-22-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write the remainder as ax+b and count the equations produced by each fact one by one.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Fact 1: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x−1 is 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say now about the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2)?
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If the remainder is ax+b, then from fact 1 only one equation, a+b=4, comes out, so a and b are not fixed.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The remainder is 4 (a constant). Because it is 4 at x=1
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: There is no information yet about x−2. Think about whether f(2) must also be 4 for the remainder to be 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is an expression of degree at most 1, and this information alone does not fix it
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You looked at both the shape of the remainder (degree at most 1) and the lack of information.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The remainder is 4x. Because the value is 4 at x=1
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There are many expressions besides 4x whose value is 4 at x=1.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It has nothing to do with x−1, so nothing can be said
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: There is already a constraint that the remainder is 4 at x=1. You do not know nothing.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Fact 2: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x−2 is also 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what is the remainder when divided by (x−1)(x−2)?
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.after: From a+b=4 and 2a+b=4, a=0 and b=4, so the remainder is the constant 4. This is because if f(1)=f(2)=4, f(x)−4 is divisible by both x−1 and x−2.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is still not fixed. There is just one more equation
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: There are now two equations. Check whether you can find a and b from the two equations.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The value is 5 at x=2, which does not match fact 2.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You judged using the two equations a+b=4 and 2a+b=4 together.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The value is 6 at x=1, which does not match fact 1.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Fact 3: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x−3 is 5. (For example, f(x)=½x²−(3/2)x+5 satisfies facts 1, 2, and 3.)
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: When this fact is added, will the remainder on division by (x−1)(x−2) change?
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.after: For the example f(x)=½x²−(3/2)x+5, f(x)−4=½(x−1)(x−2), so the remainder on division by (x−1)(x−2) stays 4. Fact 3 is information about a different point, f(3)=5.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It does not change. Fact 3 is only information about x=3
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You saw that facts 1 and 2 already fixed the remainder and fact 3 is about a different point.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It changes to 5. The fact learned last replaces the fact learned earlier
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You are seeing new information as erasing earlier information. Think about whether the earlier facts are still true.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It changes to a value between 4 and 5. Because the new fact mixes with the existing facts
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Check with the expression in the example whether the remainder mixes like an average of some values.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Facts 1 to 3 contradict each other, so no f(x) satisfies these conditions
z-m-22-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Plug 1, 2, 3 into the f(x) given as an example and check whether all three facts are true.
z-m-22-03.s.s1.reflect: With fact 1 you could not fix it, when fact 2 was added it was fixed, and fact 3 could not change what was already fixed. Try to tell apart the cases where new information changes the judgment and the cases where it does not.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three different expressions f(x)=ax²+bx+c satisfying f(1)=4 and f(2)=4. (a=0 is allowed.)
z-m-22-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write f(1) and f(2) in terms of a, b, c to make two equations.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the value of one letter (for example, a) and check that the other two letters follow.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The value a+b+c from plugging in x=1 is not 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The value 4a+2b+c from plugging in x=2 is not 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.explain: From the two conditions, b=−3a and c=4+2a, so each choice of a makes one. For example, (1, −3, 6) is x²−3x+6, (2, −6, 8) is 2x²−6x+8, (−1, 3, 2) is −x²+3x+2, and (0, 0, 4) is the constant 4. All of them have f(x)−4=a(x−1)(x−2), so the remainder on division by (x−1)(x−2) is 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.prompt: When f(1)=f(2)=4, explain why the remainder on division by (x−1)(x−2) is 4 in all three examples.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: First calculate and write what f(1) and f(2) are for each of the three expressions.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what number you can subtract from f(x) so that it becomes 0 at both x=1 and x=2.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that f(x)−4 becomes 0 at x=1 and x=2?
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you continue to the conclusion that the remainder is the constant 4?
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.model.0: Since f(1)=f(2)=4, f(x)−4 is 0 both when x=1 and when x=2. So it is divisible by (x−1)(x−2), and f(x)=(x−1)(x−2)·quotient+4, so the remainder is 4.
z-m-22-03.s.s2.because.model.1: In all three expressions f(1)=f(2)=4, so if we subtract 4, 1 and 2 become roots and (x−1)(x−2) is a factor of f(x)−4. So the remainder is 4.

z-m-22-04.title: When x²+1/x²=7, is x+1/x fixed to one value?
z-m-22-04.topic: Variations of the multiplication formula (the form x+1/x)
z-m-22-04.goal: Understand that when finding x+1/x from the value of x²+1/x², there can be two values because of the sign, and work out how things change when a condition is added.
z-m-22-04.material: x is a nonzero real number and x²+1/x²=7. "x+1/x" is read as "x plus 1 over x". Minseo said that (x+1/x)²=x²+2+1/x²=9, so x+1/x=3, and Seojun said it could be −3. Let's look at whose statement is valid and whether it changes when information is added.
z-m-22-04.thinking.1: Handling cases where the answer changes depending on the conditions
z-m-22-04.thinking.2: Looking at how a new condition changes the information
z-m-22-04.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-04.prereq.2: Two numbers that have the same value when squared (numbers that differ only in sign)
z-m-22-04.s.s1.prompt: x is a nonzero real number and x²+1/x²=7. Minseo said that (x+1/x)²=x²+2+1/x²=9, so x+1/x=3, and Seojun said it could be −3. How do you judge this?
z-m-22-04.s.s1.hint.0: Expand (x+1/x)² and write how it connects to x²+1/x².
z-m-22-04.s.s1.hint.1: Find and write all the numbers whose square is 9.
z-m-22-04.s.s1.o.a: x+1/x is fixed to 3. Because the number whose square is 9 is 3
z-m-22-04.s.s1.r.a: You saw 3 as the only number whose square is 9. Check that a negative number also becomes positive when squared.
z-m-22-04.s.s1.o.b: x+1/x is fixed to 9. Because the squared value is 9, it is 9 as it is
z-m-22-04.s.s1.r.b: You treated the value of (x+1/x)² and the value of x+1/x as the same thing.
z-m-22-04.s.s1.o.c: The candidates are 3 or −3, and we need to check for each whether a real x exists
z-m-22-04.s.s1.r.c: You are looking at both the fact that two numbers have square 9 and the fact that we need to check whether each candidate is actually possible.
z-m-22-04.s.s1.o.d: We do not know the value of x, so we cannot say anything about what number x+1/x is
z-m-22-04.s.s1.r.d: Even without knowing x, you can find the value of (x+1/x)² from the value of x²+1/x².
z-m-22-04.s.s1.explain: (x+1/x)²=x²+2+1/x²=9, so x+1/x is 3 or −3. Which of the two is possible is checked by whether such a real x actually exists.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.prompt: When there is a real x satisfying x²+1/x²=7, find and write two different values that x+1/x can take. (Write the value of x+1/x in u.)
z-m-22-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write the expression that expresses x²+1/x² in terms of u=x+1/x.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.hint.1: For each value from solving the equation in u, think about whether such an x actually exists.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.ok.c2: |u| is at least 2, so a real x can exist.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.fail.c2: For a real number x, the absolute value of x+1/x is always at least 2.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.explain: From x²+1/x²=(x+1/x)²−2=7, u²=9, so u=3 or −3. If u=3, then x²−3x+1=0, and if u=−3, then x²+3x+1=0, and both have discriminant 5, which is positive, so a real x exists.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain in a sentence or two why the value of x+1/x is not fixed to one value.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write all the values of x+1/x that satisfy (x+1/x)²=9.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check the sign of x+1/x when x is negative.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If we only know that the squared value is 9, ...
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write that there are two numbers whose square is 9?
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that the value can differ depending on the sign of x?
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.model.0: From (x+1/x)²=9, there are two numbers whose square is 9, 3 and −3, so it is not fixed to one.
z-m-22-04.s.s2.because.model.1: Only the squared value 9 is known, so both ±3 are candidates for x+1/x. If x is negative, −3 can come out too.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.prompt: New information has been added. You learned that x is positive. Now what is the value of x³+1/x³? (Reference: (x+1/x)³=x³+3(x+1/x)+1/x³)
z-m-22-04.s.s3.hint.0: First decide whether x+1/x is positive or negative when x is positive.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.hint.1: In the reference expression, write x³+1/x³ in terms of u.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.o.a: 18 or −18 (both are possible even when x is positive)
z-m-22-04.s.s3.r.a: Check what the sign of x+1/x is when x is positive.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.r.b: In (x+1/x)³, besides x³+1/x³, 3(x+1/x) is also added.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.r.c: Because x is positive, you used x+1/x=3, and subtracted 3(x+1/x)=9 from the cube of 3.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.r.d: That is the value when x is negative. When x is positive, check the sign of x+1/x.
z-m-22-04.s.s3.explain: If x>0, then x+1/x>0, so u=3. x³+1/x³=u³−3u=27−9=18. (If x<0, then u=−3 and it is −18.)

z-m-22-05.title: If only the degrees are known, are the degrees of two polynomials fixed?
z-m-22-05.topic: Degree of a polynomial (degrees of sums and products)
z-m-22-05.goal: Using two conditions on the degrees of a product and a sum to find the degrees of two polynomials, and confirm with examples what role the coefficient of the highest-degree term plays when the condition changes.
z-m-22-05.material: f(x) and g(x) are nonzero polynomials with real coefficients. The two facts below are known. (1) The degree of f(x)g(x) is 6. (2) The degree of f(x)+g(x) is 3. The degree is the exponent of the highest power among the nonzero terms. A constant (a nonzero number) has degree 0. Let's look at whether the known facts let us fix the degrees of f and g, and what happens if the information changes.
z-m-22-05.thinking.1: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-22-05.thinking.2: Making examples that satisfy the conditions
z-m-22-05.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-05.prereq.1: The meaning of the degree and the highest-degree term of a polynomial
z-m-22-05.prereq.2: Experience with how the highest-degree term is determined in the sum and product of two polynomials
z-m-22-05.s.s1.prompt: f(x) and g(x) are nonzero polynomials with real coefficients. Can the degrees of the two polynomials be fixed from the facts alone that the degree of the product f(x)g(x) is 6 and the degree of the sum f(x)+g(x) is 3?
z-m-22-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the pairs whose two degrees add up to 6, such as (6,0), (5,1), (4,2), (3,3).
z-m-22-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each pair, check one by one what the degree of f(x)+g(x) would be.
z-m-22-05.s.s1.o.a: One has degree 6 and the other is a constant of degree 0. Because the product has degree 6
z-m-22-05.s.s1.r.a: You used only the degree 6 of the product and did not use the degree 3 of the sum. Check what the degree of the sum is for (degree 6, degree 0).
z-m-22-05.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be fixed. There are several pairs with product degree 6, like (4, 2) or (5, 1)
z-m-22-05.s.s1.r.b: There are several pairs with product degree 6, but did you filter the candidates with the condition that the sum has degree 3?
z-m-22-05.s.s1.o.c: Only one has degree 3 and the other has a degree lower than 3. Because the sum has degree 3
z-m-22-05.s.s1.r.c: You used only the degree 3 of the sum and did not use the degree 6 of the product. Check what degree the product of a degree-3 expression and an expression of lower degree has.
z-m-22-05.s.s1.o.d: Both are degree 3. The other pairs cannot have a sum of degree 3
z-m-22-05.s.s1.r.d: You filtered the candidates using both conditions, the degree of the product and the degree of the sum.
z-m-22-05.s.s1.explain: The product has degree 6, so (sum of degrees)=6. If the two degrees are different, the degree of the sum is the degree of the larger one (4 or more) and cannot be 3, so the two degrees must be the same, and both are degree 3.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.prompt: Let's make f(x) and g(x) with product degree 6 and sum degree 3 by writing only the highest-degree terms. Let the degree of f be m with highest-degree coefficient p, and the degree of g be n with highest-degree coefficient q. Find two different examples. (Swapping f and g gives the same example.)
z-m-22-05.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a pair whose two degrees add up to 6 and then work out the degree of the sum.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check what happens when the degrees are equal and you add the coefficients of the highest-degree terms.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.var.p: The coefficient p of the highest-degree term of f
z-m-22-05.s.s2.var.q: The coefficient q of the highest-degree term of g
z-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The degrees are integers that are at least 0.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The degrees must be integers that are at least 0.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The coefficients of the highest-degree terms are not 0.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The coefficients of the highest-degree terms must not be 0.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The degree of the product is 6.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The degree of the product is the sum of the two degrees. m+n is not 6.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The degree of the sum is 3.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c4: The degree of the sum is not 3. Look at whether the highest-degree term does not disappear when the degrees are equal, and what the larger degree is when the degrees are different.
z-m-22-05.s.s2.explain: Both degrees must be 3, and the coefficients p and q of the highest-degree terms must be nonzero with p+q≠0 for the sum to keep degree 3. Example: if p=q=1, then f=x³+…, g=x³+…, and the sum is 2x³+…. If p=1, q=−1, the highest-degree term disappears and the sum has degree lower than 3.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.prompt: The condition has changed. The degree of the product is still 6, and the degree of the sum f(x)+g(x) is said to be 2. What will the degrees of the two polynomials be?
z-m-22-05.s.s3.hint.0: Look at how the term of the highest degree remains in the sum of two polynomials with different degrees.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.hint.1: Make one example and check the degrees of the product and the sum yourself.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.o.a: (4, 2) or (2, 4). The sum has degree 2, so the lower one has degree 2
z-m-22-05.s.s3.r.a: If the degrees are different, the degree of the sum becomes the higher degree (4). The sum cannot have degree 2.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.o.b: Both have degree 3, and the sum of the coefficients is 0 so that the two highest-degree terms disappear
z-m-22-05.s.s3.r.b: You used the fact that the highest-degree term can disappear only when the degrees are equal.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.o.c: Both have degree 3, and the sum of the coefficients of the highest-degree terms is not 0
z-m-22-05.s.s3.r.c: If the highest-degree term remains, the sum has degree 3. Think about what must happen for the sum to have degree 2.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.o.d: No f(x) and g(x) satisfy these conditions
z-m-22-05.s.s3.r.d: Check directly with, for example, f=x³+x², g=−x³+x.
z-m-22-05.s.s3.explain: If the degrees are different, the degree of the sum is the larger one (4 or more) and cannot be 2. So both must be degree 3 and the highest-degree terms must disappear. Example: if f=x³+x², g=−x³+x, the product has degree 6 and the sum is x²+x, which has degree 2.

z-m-22-06.title: When there are two conditions but a and b are still not fixed
z-m-22-06.topic: The factor theorem and determining coefficients (independence of information)
z-m-22-06.goal: Judge whether the unknowns are fixed not by the number of conditions but by the number of independent pieces of information, and pick out conditions that are the same statement written differently or conditions that are always true.
z-m-22-06.material: f(x)=x³+ax²+bx−6, where a and b are real constants. The statement "the remainder on division by a linear expression is 0" and the statement "that linear expression is a factor of f(x)" mean the same thing. Let's look at whether the known facts about f(x) fix the values of a and b as a pair.
z-m-22-06.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-22-06.thinking.1: Telling apart the same information and new information
z-m-22-06.thinking.2: Refuting a claim with counterexamples (several pairs)
z-m-22-06.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-06.prereq.1: Know that if the remainder of a polynomial divided by a linear expression is 0, then that linear expression is a factor (it divides evenly)
z-m-22-06.prereq.2: Experience with the conditions under which the solution of simultaneous equations is fixed to one
z-m-22-06.s.s1.prompt: For f(x)=x³+ax²+bx−6 (a and b are real numbers), find three different pairs (a, b) that make x−1 a factor of f(x).
z-m-22-06.s.s1.hint.0: First decide what value of x makes x−1 equal to 0, and write what f must be at that value.
z-m-22-06.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one a and then find what b must be.
z-m-22-06.s.s1.ok.c1: The value of f at x=1 is 0.
z-m-22-06.s.s1.fail.c1: If x−1 is a factor, the value 1+a+b−6 from plugging in x=1 must be 0.
z-m-22-06.s.s1.explain: If x−1 is a factor, then f(1)=1+a+b−6=0, so a+b=5. There are as many pairs with sum 5 as you like, such as (0, 5), (1, 4), (−1, 6), (2, 3). One condition does not fix a and b to one pair.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.prompt: f(x)=x³+ax²+bx−6. Choose all the sets below for which those facts alone fix (a, b) as a single pair.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.hint.0: For each set, rewrite the two facts as equations of the form "f(some number)=value".
z-m-22-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the two equations are different pieces of information or whether one comes directly from the other.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.o.a: x−1 is a factor of f(x). The remainder when f(x) is divided by x−1 is 0.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.r.a: Did you compare whether the two sentences are the same fact? If they say the same thing, only one equation is produced.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.r.b: These are values at two different points, so two independent equations in a and b are produced.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.o.c: f(0)=−6. x−1 is a factor of f(x).
z-m-22-06.s.s2.r.c: Write directly what equation f(0) gives in terms of a and b.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.o.d: Both x−1 and x+1 are factors of f(x).
z-m-22-06.s.s2.r.d: You saw that you get two equations saying that the values at x=1 and x=−1 are both 0.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.o.e: x−1 is a factor of f(x). The remainder when f(x) is divided by x+2 is −6.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.r.e: You checked that information at two different points produces two equations.
z-m-22-06.s.s2.explain: a: both sentences say f(1)=0, so there is only one equation. c: f(0)=−6 is the constant term −6 of the expression, so it is always true regardless of a and b, which means it gives no new information and only f(1)=0 remains. b: a+b=5, 2a+b=−1 → (a, b)=(−6, 11). d: a+b=5, a−b=7 → (6, −1). e: from f(1)=0, f(−2)=−6, a+b=5, 2a−b=4 → (3, 2).
z-m-22-06.s.s2.acc.0: b and d were chosen correctly. For e, it is also information at two different points, so solve it yourself and check whether a single pair is fixed.
z-m-22-06.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, "There are two conditions, f(0)=−6 and x−1 being a factor, so a and b are fixed." Write what you think about this claim, with reasons.
z-m-22-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write directly whether a and b appear when you calculate f(0).
z-m-22-06.s.s3.hint.1: Connect to the result of s1 how many pairs (a, b) remain when there is only f(1)=0.
z-m-22-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in which part of the expression f(0)=−6 is already known?
z-m-22-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write how many conditions effectively remain as a result?
z-m-22-06.s.s3.model.0: f(0)=−6 means that the constant term in the expression of f is −6, so it always holds whatever a and b are. So it is not new information, and effectively the only condition is the single one, f(1)=0.
z-m-22-06.s.s3.model.1: That the constant term is −6 is already written in the expression. It gives no information about a and b, so with only the single fact that x−1 is a factor, pairs with a+b=5 keep remaining.

z-m-22-07.title: How many ways can (x²+ax+b)(x+c) be the same cubic expression?
z-m-22-07.goal: Systematically find the several solutions that make an expression written as a product equal to a given cubic expression, and explain whether the candidates were checked completely and why a solution is eliminated by a mismatch in one coefficient.
z-m-22-07.material: An equation that holds whatever value you plug in for x is called an identity. For two polynomials to be equal as an identity, the coefficients of terms of the same degree must all be equal. Now let's think about the integers a, b, c that make the following an identity. (x²+ax+b)(x+c)=x³+2x²−5x−6. The fact that the right side equals (x+1)(x−2)(x+3) has been left unsaid on purpose.
z-m-22-07.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-07.prereq.2: Finding all the divisors of 6 (including positive and negative)
z-m-22-07.s.s1.prompt: Find three different triples of integers a, b, c that make the following an equation that holds for any value of x (an identity).  (x²+ax+b)(x+c)=x³+2x²−5x−6
z-m-22-07.s.s1.hint.0: Expand the left side and compare the coefficients of x³, x², x, and the constant term with the right side one by one.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.hint.1: First choose an integer c that satisfies bc=−6, and then find the other letters.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.fail.c2: The coefficient of x² (a+c) after expanding the left side is not 2.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.fail.c3: The coefficient of x (b+ac) after expanding the left side is not −5.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.fail.c4: The constant term (bc) after expanding the left side is not −6.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.explain: Expanding the left side gives x³+(a+c)x²+(b+ac)x+bc, so a+c=2, b+ac=−5, bc=−6. The integer solutions are only the three (a, b, c)=(1, −6, 1), (4, 3, −2), (−1, −2, 3). This corresponds to which linear expression (x+c) you pick out of x³+2x²−5x−6=(x+1)(x−2)(x+3).
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.prompt: Explain how you chose the candidates for c while finding the solutions, and why you can say there are no more.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.hint.0: List all the integers c that satisfy bc=−6.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.hint.1: For each c, find b and a, and then check whether b+ac is −5.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the criterion for choosing candidates (the product is −6)?
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write which of the candidates remain and which are eliminated, with reasons?
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.model.0: Since bc=−6, I chose c from the divisors of 6 (±1, ±2, ±3, ±6), found a and b for each, and checked up to the coefficient of x, and only c=1, −2, 3 worked. These are all the candidates, so there are no more.
z-m-22-07.s.s1.because.model.1: Since bc=−6, the only integers c can be are divisors of 6. I checked all 8 divisors and only three remained, so I found them all without missing any.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.prompt: This is a solution by a student who tried c=2. Choose the wrong line.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether the value found in each line matches the expression in the line before.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write which degrees' coefficients you must compare to say two polynomials are equal.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.line.0: Expanding the left side gives x³+(a+c)x²+(b+ac)x+bc, so a+c=2, b+ac=−5, bc=−6 must hold.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.line.1: Let's say c=2. From bc=−6, b=−3, and from a+c=2, a=0.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.line.3: Even though −3 and −5 are different, the coefficient of x² and the constant term match, so the two expressions are equal. So c=2 is also a solution.
z-m-22-07.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is wrong. For two polynomials to be equal, the coefficients of all degrees must be equal. If c=2, the coefficient of x is −3, which differs from −5, so it is not a solution. The calculations in lines 1 to 3 are correct.

z-m-22-08.title: For three numbers whose sum is 6, is the sum of their squares fixed too?
z-m-22-08.topic: Multiplication formulas (the sum of squares of three letters)
z-m-22-08.goal: Show with counterexamples that the sum of squares is not fixed when only the sum is known, and use expressions to sort out what information would fix it.
z-m-22-08.material: For real numbers a, b, c, it is known that a+b+c=6. Let's see whether this fact lets us know the value of a²+b²+c², and if not, what else is needed. (a² is read as "a squared".)
z-m-22-08.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-22-08.thinking.2: Sorting out the extra information that is needed
z-m-22-08.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-08.prereq.2: Experience calculating the value of an expression by plugging in numbers
z-m-22-08.s.s1.prompt: For real numbers a, b, c, only a+b+c=6 is known. What is the value of a²+b²+c²?
z-m-22-08.s.s1.hint.0: Choose any three numbers whose sum is 6 and calculate a²+b²+c².
z-m-22-08.s.s1.hint.1: Choose another set of three numbers and compare whether the same value comes out.
z-m-22-08.s.s1.o.a: It is fixed at 36. You can find it right away by squaring 6
z-m-22-08.s.s1.r.a: You thought (a+b+c)² is the same as a²+b²+c². Check what extra terms appear when you expand (a+b+c)².
z-m-22-08.s.s1.o.b: It is fixed at 12. The standard is the value from splitting 6 into three equal parts
z-m-22-08.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the case a=b=c=2. Check whether other cases give the same value.
z-m-22-08.s.s1.o.c: It is not fixed. The value depends on a, b, c
z-m-22-08.s.s1.r.c: You saw that even with the same sum, the sum of squares can change if a, b, c change.
z-m-22-08.s.s1.o.d: It is fixed, but it cannot be calculated with the information known now
z-m-22-08.s.s1.r.d: If it is fixed, the same value must come out in any example with sum 6. Test it with two examples.
z-m-22-08.s.s1.explain: If the example with sum 6 is (2,2,2), then a²+b²+c²=12, and if it is (6,0,0), it is 36, so the value is not fixed to one.
z-m-22-08.s.s2.prompt: Make two examples of three numbers with a+b+c=6 but different values of a²+b²+c², and show that the value is not fixed.
z-m-22-08.s.s2.hint.0: Make three numbers whose sum is 6, then calculate the sum of squares and write them in a table.
z-m-22-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose two examples whose sums of squares are different.
z-m-22-08.s.s2.explain: For example, (2,2,2) gives 12, (6,0,0) gives 36, (1,2,3) gives 14, and (4,1,1) gives 18. Even with the same sum, the sums of squares are different, so a+b+c=6 alone does not fix it. Two examples that give the same value (for example, (1,2,3) and (3,2,1)) were not counted as different examples.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.prompt: In addition to a+b+c=6, which of the following facts, if also known, would fix the value of a²+b²+c² to one value? Choose all of them.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each fact, look for two examples with different a²+b²+c² even when that fact is known.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write down the expanded form of (a+b+c)² and check which fact fills in the blank in that expression.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.r.a: Look for an example where abc is the same but a²+b²+c² is different. (For example, (6,0,0) and (3,3,0) with abc=0)
z-m-22-08.s.s3.r.b: You saw how it connects to a²+b²+c² in the expanded form of (a+b+c)².
z-m-22-08.s.s3.o.c: The value of c (for example, c=0)
z-m-22-08.s.s3.r.c: Check whether, even when c is fixed, a and b can keep changing while satisfying a+b=6−c.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.r.d: You calculated how a²+b²+c² and ab+bc+ca appear when this expression is expanded.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.o.e: The fact that a²+b²+c² is at least 12
z-m-22-08.s.s3.r.e: Think about whether this is new information, since it already holds in any example with sum 6.
z-m-22-08.s.s3.explain: Since (a+b+c)²=a²+b²+c²+2(ab+bc+ca), if you know ab+bc+ca, then a²+b²+c²=36−2(ab+bc+ca) is fixed. Since (a−b)²+(b−c)²+(c−a)²=3(a²+b²+c²)−36, knowing this value also fixes it. The value of abc, the value of c, and "at least 12" do not fix the value.

z-m-22-09.title: From which line did the calculation of three polynomials go differently?
z-m-22-09.topic: Addition and subtraction of polynomials (the minus sign before a parenthesis)
z-m-22-09.goal: Find the first wrong line in a solution, compare ways to check the result without recalculating it, and explain the corrected result.
z-m-22-09.material: There are polynomials A=x²−3x+2, B=2x²+x−4, C=x−5. A student wrote out line by line a solution for finding 2A−(B−C), and wrote the result as −6x+13. All coefficients are integers and x is a letter.
z-m-22-09.thinking.1: Comparing ways to check an answer
z-m-22-09.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-09.prereq.1: Addition and subtraction of polynomials and combining like terms
z-m-22-09.prereq.2: Finding the value of an expression by plugging a number into a polynomial
z-m-22-09.s.s1.prompt: This is a solution for finding 2A−(B−C) when A=x²−3x+2, B=2x²+x−4, C=x−5. Choose the first wrong line.
z-m-22-09.s.s1.hint.0: Recalculate each line using only the result of the line before it.
z-m-22-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write directly how each term inside the parentheses changes when you remove the parentheses after a minus sign.
z-m-22-09.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. When you subtract (x−5), the signs of both x and −5 change, so it should be −x+5, but −5 was left as it was. The correct B−C is 2x²+1. Lines 3 and 4 correctly continue from the result of the previous line, so the first wrong line is line 2.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.prompt: The result came out as −6x+13. Which method is suitable for quickly checking whether this result has an error, without rewriting the solution?
z-m-22-09.s.s2.hint.0: Use the fact that if the expressions are correct, the two expressions must have the same value whatever number you plug in for x.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.hint.1: First plug x=1 into A, B, C to find their values, and compare with the resulting expression.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.o.a: If the result has a simple shape like a linear expression, it can be considered correct
z-m-22-09.s.s2.r.a: An expression being simple is not evidence that it is right. A wrong calculation can also give a simple expression.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.o.b: Plug the same number into x and compare the values of the original expression and the resulting expression
z-m-22-09.s.s2.r.b: You checked the result by connecting it directly to the original expression.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.o.c: If the x² term disappeared in the result, the rest of the calculation was probably right too
z-m-22-09.s.s2.r.c: Even if the x² term disappeared, there can still be mistakes in the linear term or the constant term.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.o.d: If the result has fewer terms than the original expression, it was probably right
z-m-22-09.s.s2.r.d: The number of terms has nothing to do with whether the result is right or wrong.
z-m-22-09.s.s2.explain: If you plug in x=1, A=0, B=−1, C=−4, so the original expression is 0−(−1+4)=−3. But −6+13=7, so they differ. Plugging in the same value of x and comparing lets you find the error quickly. The correct result −6x+3 is −3 at x=1.
z-m-22-09.s.s3.prompt: Explain to a friend where this solution is wrong, and write the correct result as well.
z-m-22-09.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite −(x−5) in line 2 by changing the sign of each term.
z-m-22-09.s.s3.hint.1: Recalculate 2A−(B−C) from the beginning with the corrected B−C.
z-m-22-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the signs change for all the terms inside the parentheses after the minus sign?
z-m-22-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check the result from beginning to end after fixing it?
z-m-22-09.s.s3.model.0: In line 2, when removing the parentheses of −(x−5), the sign of −5 should also change to +5, but I wrote −5. B−C=2x²+1 and the final result is −6x+3.
z-m-22-09.s.s3.model.1: A minus sign before a parenthesis changes the signs of all the terms inside. If you subtract (x−5), it becomes −x+5, so B−C=2x²+1, and so 2A−(B−C)=3−6x.

z-m-22-10.title: If the first number in the table changes, what was divided?
z-m-22-10.topic: Synthetic division (the first number depends on the divisor)
z-m-22-10.goal: Find the wrong line in the table, check by a value which linear expression the remainder you found came from, and explain the correct quotient and remainder.
z-m-22-10.material: This is a student's solution for finding the quotient and remainder when f(x)=2x³+5x²−x+4 is divided by the linear expression x+3. The student used synthetic division and wrote the result as "quotient 2x²+11x+32, remainder 100". All coefficients are integers.
z-m-22-10.thinking.1: Interpreting the meaning of the value you found
z-m-22-10.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-10.prereq.1: Dividing by the linear expression x−k using synthetic division
z-m-22-10.prereq.2: Finding the value of a polynomial by plugging in a number
z-m-22-10.s.s1.prompt: This is a student's synthetic division solution for dividing f(x)=2x³+5x²−x+4 by x+3. Choose the wrong line.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.hint.0: Redo the calculation of each line using only the numbers from the line before it.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.hint.1: Solve directly for the value of x that makes the divisor 0.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.line.0: Find the quotient and remainder of dividing f(x)=2x³+5x²−x+4 by x+3.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.line.1: From x+3=0, x=3, so write 3 on the left side of the synthetic division.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.line.2: Write the coefficients 2, 5, −1, 4, bring down 2, multiply by 3 to get 6, and add it to 5 to get 11.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.line.3: Add 11×3=33 to −1 to get 32, and add 32×3=96 to 4 to get 100.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.line.4: The quotient is 2x²+11x+32 and the remainder is 100.
z-m-22-10.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. If x+3=0, then x=−3. Writing 3 makes it a calculation of dividing by x−3. Lines 3 to 5 are calculations based on the 3 written on the left, so they are correct as calculations on their own.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.prompt: You want to check the remainder 100 that the student found. To check the result of dividing by x+3, which value should you calculate and compare with 100?
z-m-22-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write the value of x that makes the divisor x+3 equal to 0, and plug that value into f.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what it means if f(3) calculated is equal to the student's 100.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.o.a: Find f(3) and compare it with the student's remainder 100
z-m-22-10.s.s2.r.a: f(3)=100, so it looks the same as the student's answer. But think about which linear expression's remainder f(3) tells you.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.o.b: Find f(0) and compare it with the student's remainder 100
z-m-22-10.s.s2.r.b: f(0)=4 is the constant term. Think about how it connects to the divisor x+3.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.o.c: Find f(−3) and compare it with the student's remainder 100
z-m-22-10.s.s2.r.c: You tried to find the value of f at the value of x that makes the divisor 0.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.o.d: Find f(1) and compare the sum of the coefficients with the student's remainder 100
z-m-22-10.s.s2.r.d: f(1)=2+5−1+4=10 is the sum of the coefficients. Think about its relationship with the divisor x+3.
z-m-22-10.s.s2.explain: f(−3)=2(−27)+5(9)−(−3)+4=−2. The student's 100 equals f(3), so it corresponds to the remainder on division by x−3. So the remainder on division by x+3 is not 100.
z-m-22-10.s.s3.prompt: Explain what the "remainder 100" the student found is actually the value of, and write the correct quotient and remainder on division by x+3.
z-m-22-10.s.s3.hint.0: Leave the student's table as it is and write which linear expression the number 3 written on the left makes equal to 0.
z-m-22-10.s.s3.hint.1: Change the number written on the left for dividing by x+3 and recalculate the table.
z-m-22-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write which division the student's 3 corresponds to?
z-m-22-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check up to the quotient (2x²−x+2) in the correct table?
z-m-22-10.s.s3.model.0: 100 is f(3), so it is the remainder when dividing by x−3. To divide by x+3, you must write −3 on the left, and the quotient is 2x²−x+2 and the remainder is −2.
z-m-22-10.s.s3.model.1: The student used x=3, so they found the result of dividing by x−3. The correct table writes −3 and calculates to get quotient 2x²−x+2 and remainder −2.

z-m-22-11.title: Which way is good for calculating 997×1003?
z-m-22-11.goal: Pick out the correct transformations of a calculation that uses multiplication formulas, make numbers of your own for which the method works well, and judge the cases where it does not work or is inconvenient.
z-m-22-11.material: You want to calculate 997×1003 without multiplying vertically on paper. Three friends each suggested a different method. In this task, you think about whether each method is right or wrong and for which numbers it is convenient. All numbers are natural numbers.
z-m-22-11.thinking.0: Comparing the correctness of several calculation methods
z-m-22-11.thinking.1: Making examples that fit the conditions
z-m-22-11.thinking.2: Judging the range where a method applies
z-m-22-11.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-11.prereq.2: Experience expanding a product with the distributive law
z-m-22-11.s.s1.prompt: You want to calculate 997×1003 by changing it using a multiplication formula or distribution. Choose all the transformations below that give the same value (are correct).
z-m-22-11.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate each expression all the way to its value and compare them with each other.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.hint.1: Expand (1000−3)(1000+3) yourself and write what happens to the middle term.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.r.a: You used the fact that the two numbers are at the same distance from 1000.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.r.b: In (A−B)(A+B)=A²−B², B² does not become B×2. Check what B² is when B=3.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.r.c: Expand and check what the sign of B² is in (A−B)(A+B).
z-m-22-11.s.s1.r.d: This is a method that sees 997 as 1000−3 and uses the distributive law.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.r.e: You got the same result by expanding the four terms directly without using a multiplication formula.
z-m-22-11.s.s1.explain: a and e use (A−B)(A+B)=A²−B² to get 1000²−9=999991. d is 1003000−3009=999991, which is the same. b is 1000²−6=999994 and c is 1000²+9=1000009, so their values are different.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.prompt: Make three different products of two natural numbers that are easy to calculate in your head using the multiplication formula (A−B)(A+B)=A²−B². Conditions: the average of the two numbers p<q is a multiple of 10 (for example, the average of 997 and 1003 is 1000), and the difference between the two numbers is at most 10.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.hint.0: First find the middle value (average) of the two numbers and the distance from the middle to each number.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a number that is a multiple of 10 as the average, and make two numbers that are the same distance above and below it.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.ok.c1: p is at least 10 and p<q.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be at least 10 and p<q must hold.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.ok.c2: p and q are natural numbers.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.fail.c2: p and q must be natural numbers.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.ok.c3: The average is a multiple of 10.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.fail.c3: The average (p+q)/2 of the two numbers is not a multiple of 10.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.ok.c4: The difference between the two numbers is at most 10.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.fail.c4: The difference between the two numbers is greater than 10.
z-m-22-11.s.s2.explain: If the average is M and the distance from the average is d, then p×q=(M−d)(M+d)=M²−d². Examples: 48×52=50²−2²=2496, 28×32=30²−2²=896, 95×105=100²−5²=9975, 997×1003=1000²−3²=999991.
z-m-22-11.s.s3.prompt: Can the same method be used when p+q is odd, as in 997×1002? Write whether it works or not, the reason, and what you think about whether it is practical for mental math.
z-m-22-11.s.s3.hint.0: Find the middle value of 997 and 1002.
z-m-22-11.s.s3.hint.1: Say what inconvenience arises when the middle value is not an integer.
z-m-22-11.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The average of 997 and 1002 is ...
z-m-22-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write knowing that the average is not an integer?
z-m-22-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your conclusion of works/does not work connect to the reason?
z-m-22-11.s.s3.model.0: It works. The average of 997 and 1002 is 999.5 and the distance is 2.5, so it can be written as 999.5²−2.5². But these are squares of decimals, so they are inconvenient for mental math.
z-m-22-11.s.s3.model.1: The sum is odd, so the average is not an integer. The method that uses only integers does not work, and it is easier to split it up like 997×1002=997×1000+997×2.

z-m-22-12.title: How far must x⁴−4 be split before it is finished?
z-m-22-12.topic: Factoring (complete factoring depending on the range of coefficients)
z-m-22-12.goal: Understand that the judgment that factoring is "finished" depends on the range of coefficients, and decide how to write the answer when no range is given.
z-m-22-12.material: There are three solutions for x⁴−4. Solution ①: (x²−2)(x²+2), Solution ②: (x−√2)(x+√2)(x²+2), Solution ③: (x−√2)(x+√2)(x−√2i)(x+√2i). All three solutions give x⁴−4 when expanded. In factoring, the phrase "does not split any further" depends on which numbers are allowed as coefficients.
z-m-22-12.thinking.0: Telling apart conclusions that depend on conditions
z-m-22-12.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-12.prereq.2: The basic meaning of complex numbers (the imaginary unit i, i²=−1)
z-m-22-12.s.s1.prompt: There are three solutions that factor x⁴−4. Solution ①: (x²−2)(x²+2). Solution ②: (x−√2)(x+√2)(x²+2). Solution ③: (x−√2)(x+√2)(x−√2i)(x+√2i). Choose all the correct statements below. (i is the imaginary unit and i²=−1.)
z-m-22-12.s.s1.hint.0: Expand the factors of each solution and check whether you get x⁴−4.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.hint.1: Think one by one about whether each factor splits further with coefficients in that range.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.o.a: If coefficients are limited to integers, solution ① cannot be split further
z-m-22-12.s.s1.r.a: You know that the "end" is decided by which range of coefficients you use.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.o.b: If coefficients are allowed up to the real numbers, solution ① is not yet fully split
z-m-22-12.s.s1.r.b: You saw that in the real numbers, x²−2 splits into two linear expressions.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.o.c: x²+2 splits into (x−√2)(x+√2) in the real numbers
z-m-22-12.s.s1.r.c: Expanding (x−√2)(x+√2) gives x²−2. Check whether it is the same as x²+2.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.o.d: Whatever range of coefficients you use, solution ① is the final factorization
z-m-22-12.s.s1.r.d: There are expressions that can be split more as the range of coefficients gets wider.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.o.e: If complex numbers are allowed, x²+2 also splits into a product of two linear expressions
z-m-22-12.s.s1.r.e: You saw that the solutions of x²+2=0 are imaginary, so in the complex numbers it splits into linear expressions.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.explain: The "end" of factoring depends on the range of coefficients. In the integers it is (x²−2)(x²+2), in the real numbers it is (x−√2)(x+√2)(x²+2), and in the complex numbers it is a product of four linear expressions. x²+2 does not split further in the real numbers, and (x−√2)(x+√2)=x²−2.
z-m-22-12.s.s1.acc.0: a and b were chosen correctly. If you also think about the range that uses complex numbers (e), it becomes more complete.
z-m-22-12.s.s2.prompt: On a test, the question only says "Factor x⁴−4" and the range of coefficients is not written. How would you write your answer? Write it with reasons.
z-m-22-12.s.s2.hint.0: First write which range of coefficients each of ①, ②, ③ is an answer for.
z-m-22-12.s.s2.hint.1: If you cannot know which one the grader expects, think about what it would be good to write in the answer.
z-m-22-12.s.s2.placeholder: Example: There is no range, so ...
z-m-22-12.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state which range of coefficients you assumed in your answer?
z-m-22-12.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing how things differ in other ranges?
z-m-22-12.s.s2.model.0: I will state the range separately. In the integers, it is (x²−2)(x²+2), and if the real numbers are allowed, I will write (x−√2)(x+√2)(x²+2).
z-m-22-12.s.s2.model.1: If nothing is said, it is often taken as the range of integer coefficients, so I will write (x²−2)(x²+2), and add that if more is allowed, using √2 it splits further.

z-m-22-13.title: What can we know about the coefficients without expanding?
z-m-22-13.topic: Coefficients of a polynomial and values when numbers are plugged in
z-m-22-13.goal: Sort out which relationships among coefficients you can know and which you cannot from the values obtained by plugging in numbers, make expressions of your own that satisfy the relationship, and explain the reason in easy words.
z-m-22-13.material: If you expand f(x)=(2x−1)⁵, terms from x⁵ down to the constant term appear. Call the coefficient of each term c5, c4, c3, c2, c1, c0 (c5 is the coefficient of x⁵ and c0 is the constant term). In this task, without expanding, we think about what we can know and what we cannot know from the values obtained by plugging in only 0, 1, −1 for x. (2x−1)⁵ is read as "2x minus 1, to the fifth power".
z-m-22-13.thinking.0: Telling apart what is possible and what is impossible
z-m-22-13.thinking.1: Making expressions that satisfy the conditions
z-m-22-13.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level of this production batch and is not a grade set by the curriculum. Assume you have already learned the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (the four operations of polynomials, division identities, and factoring).
z-m-22-13.prereq.1: Finding the value of an expression by plugging a number into a polynomial
z-m-22-13.prereq.2: The sign rule for powers of (−1)
z-m-22-13.s.s1.prompt: Suppose you expanded f(x)=(2x−1)⁵ and wrote f(x)=c5x⁵+c4x⁴+c3x³+c2x²+c1x+c0. Choose all the things you can find using only the values obtained by plugging in 0, 1, −1 for x without expanding.
z-m-22-13.s.s1.hint.0: Write how the expanded form of f(x) becomes simpler when you plug in x=0, 1, −1.

z-m-22-13.s.s1.o.a: The sum of all the coefficients c5+c4+c3+c2+c1+c0

z-m-22-13.s.s1.explain: At x=1, f(1)=c5+…+c0=(2−1)⁵=1, and at x=−1, f(−1)=−c5+c4−c3+c2−c1+c0=(−3)⁵=−243. The sum of the odd-degree coefficients is (f(1)−f(−1))/2=122. The coefficients alternate in sign (32, −80, 80, −40, 10, −1), so the sum of the absolute values is |f(−1)|=243. c3 or c4 cannot be found individually.

z-m-22-13.s.s2.prompt: For the cubic expression f(x)=x³+ax²+bx+c, make three different expressions in which the total sum of the coefficients is 0 and the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms (x³, x) is also 0.
z-m-22-13.s.s2.hint.0: Write the total sum of the coefficients and the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms each as an equation in a, b, c.
z-m-22-13.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one letter first and find the others.

z-m-22-13.s.s2.fail.c1: The total sum of the coefficients 1+a+b+c is not 0.
z-m-22-13.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms is 0.
z-m-22-13.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum 1+b of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms (x³, x) is not 0.
z-m-22-13.s.s2.explain: b=−1 and c=−a. Examples: if a=0, x³−x; if a=1, x³+x²−x−1; if a=2, x³+2x²−x−2. These expressions have f(1)=0 and f(−1)=0, so they all have (x−1)(x+1) as a factor, and x³+ax²−x−a=(x−1)(x+1)(x+a).
